_what_this_is: The states the two update surfaces must agree about, written once and driven
through BOTH of them: the home card (cabinet/dashboard/src/lib/updates.ts,
updateHeadline + refusalToShow + applyTarget, vitest) and the briefing line
(framework/frontdoor/run_briefing._update_notice, pytest). Each reader gets
the SAME bytes -- `state` is written verbatim as .updates/state.json, and the
card fixture is derived from these same fields exactly as `cabinet-update.sh
status --json` derives its report from them.
`resolved` IS PART OF THE FIXTURE (A5.17). Both surfaces consume ONE resolved
refusal and nothing else: the verdict standing on the WAITING bundle, or --
when nothing waits -- the newest verdict nothing has overtaken. The card is
handed it by `status --json`; the briefing resolves it itself. So each case
declares what the resolution must be, hand-derived from the contract, and
BOTH suites assert it: pytest against the briefing's resolver over these very
bytes, vitest by feeding the card exactly what the report would carry. Before
round 6 the card re-derived the scoping itself from `state`, which is what
made the two surfaces able to disagree about which bundle a refusal was
about at all.
WHY IT IS ONE FILE. Both sides carried the comment 'two surfaces reading one
state file must not be able to disagree' while the third of the three rules
was written on the card only: `refusalToShow` opened with `applying -> null`
and `_update_refusal_line` had no applying guard, so through every retry of a
digest-mismatch refusal the card said 'Taking an update' and the briefing said
'Update refused'. Two independently-authored fixture sets cannot catch that --
each side proves only itself. One fixture set, two readers, can.
`agree.kind` is the classification both sentences must land on; the wording
differs on purpose (one is a card headline, one is a briefing line), so what
is asserted is the kind, the bundle every sha-shaped token in the sentence
names, and any wording the two genuinely share. Add a state here and BOTH
suites start asserting it. The WHOLE product of the six axes these readers
branch on is update_surface_oracle.json; these seven are the argued cases,
kept because a table cannot say why a state was ever in doubt.

cases.name: refused, same sha, busy -- timing, never a verdict on the bytes
refused, some OTHER sha -- never silences the one that is waiting
applying, the same bundle still waiting, its refusal still on record
_why: The retry the card is designed for: it KEEPS Apply for a digest-mismatch,
unreadable or busy refusal, tapping it moves phase to `applying` with that
same sha still in `last_refusal` (the write carries that field) and the
bundle still in the inbox until the apply lands. Durable, too: a killed
apply leaves `phase: applying` and its snapshot on disk. This is the state
the two surfaces disagreed about until 2026-09-09.

cases.name: applied, nothing waiting, and the refusal it overtook still on record
_why: The end of the busy race the `phase != applying` guard exists for, driven
through the real record_refusal and the real write_state: the winner takes
bbbb..., the loser records `busy` about bbbb..., the winner lands, and
`last_refusal` is carried onto the applied document by CARRIED_STATE_FIELDS
-- deliberately, because a refusal is still true after the next thing
happens. The install IS bbbb... now, so `status --json` excludes it and
nothing is waiting. Until 2026-09-09 both surfaces answered that state with
'Update refused -- busy (bbbbbbbb)', over a Cabinet running exactly those
bytes, and went on answering it for ever: nothing clears `last_refusal`.
The `applied` case above cannot see it -- it carries no refusal, which is
the one field the carry rule guarantees will be there on any install that
has ever refused anything. A refusal speaks while it is the LAST THING THAT
HAPPENED; an apply or a rollback since has overtaken it.
